body:
@edoxthebest I tried your minimal reproduction, analyzed how minLength works and I think I found the issue. 
First of all, you are using `input type='number'` in your code, which converts the value to number. This means that whatever char you are typing, it will be a number. 
Second, looking at Angular Validators source code https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/master/packages/forms/src/validators.ts, specifically on line 287 we have the minLength function. And on line 292 we have this code : `const length: number = control.value ? control.value.length : 0;`. As our `control.value` is number, and specifically 0, the `Boolean(0)` is false, which will always resolve `length` variable with 0, thus it will always be Invalid.
So I think the solution would call toString on control.value check 
 `const value = control.value.toString();
const length: number = value ? value.length : 0;`
But this is a change in angular forms code. 
On the side note: The issue doesn't reproduce with `input type='text'` because `Boolean('0')` is true

Seeing the above-proposed solution I believe it's better to consider the following cases before implementing the solution:
1. Number with decimals. Decimal will be counted towards length
2. Negative numbers. The sign will go towards the length.
3. For large number inputs getting stored in exponential format.
4. User input 0 will have a length of 1 using control.value.toString() but input 0123 will have length 3 and not 4.
5. Performance using the toString() method.

@praveen-sivadasan 
Number (or amount) fields are very tricky. In our case we ended up dropping the input type number because it gave us a couple of problems. First of all our user didn't like that he could enter 'e' symbol. He understands that this is the way it works, but nevertheless it's shouldn't be accepted by business. Also input type number acted strange on Firefox and IE. 
We end up using a custom decimal input directive on form field (for preventing user to enter chars) with the help of HostListener, together with decimal number custom validator.

It would appear that minLength validator is intended to work with strings. And to use a floating point decimal validation, e.g. allow 2 decimal only, you could use Validators.pattern(/^\d+\.\d{2}$/) again with strings only, because if you have input type number, value "2.00" will be converted to "2" as number and it would fail the Validators.pattern validation.
I will take a look at this issue.

issue.title: fix(forms): handle numeric values properly in the validator

issue.body:
Previously, the behaviour of the `minLength` and `maxLength` validator
caused confusion, and making it appear as they work with numeric values.
This commit fixes this, by always passing the validation when a numeric value
is used.

BREAKING CHANGES:

* The `minLength` and `maxLength` validators now verify that a value has
numeric `length` property and invoke validation only if that's the case.
Previously, falsey values without the length property (such as `0` or
`false` values) were triggering validation errors. If your code relies on
the old behavior, you can include other validators such as [min][1] or
[requiredTrue][2] to the list of validators for a particular field.

[1]: https://angular.io/api/forms/Validators#min
[2]: https://angular.io/api/forms/Validators#requiredTrue

Closes #35591

body: It should also be noted that the current `minlength` and `maxlength` do not actually work for number fields anyway. The validator will always indicate no error for a non-zero number and error for a zero number, whatever the setting of the validator. So there is no point in using it in an application.
